svastivācana
------------------------------------------
Before beginning any auspicious religious rite, some ब्राह्मणस्, elders and sumaṅgalis (married women whose husbands are alive) are invited, honoured and then requested to say ‘May it be auspicious!’
This is called स्वस्तिवाचन or svastyayana.
This is a custom prevalent even now.

Svarloka
------------------------------------------
Also known as स्वर्ग, it is situated between the sun and the ध्रुव-नक्षत्र (the pole-star). It is ruled by इन्द्र (the king of gods) with his capital at Amarāvati. Gods and extremely meritorious human beings live here. It is the Hindu concept of हेअवेन्.

svagatabheda
(‘internal distinctions’)
------------------------------------------
See SAJĀTĪYABHEDA.

svarūpalakṣaṇa
(‘essential characteristic’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Advaita Vedānta the integral or essential characteristic (svarūpalakṣaṇa) of ब्रह्मन् is ‘sat-cit-आनन्द’ (existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss) whereas the तटस्थलक्षण (accidental characteristics) is responsible for च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and dissolution of this world. An example can make these ideas more clear.
While indicating the होउसे of Devadatta, one can point out the direction of its location through the extended branch of a mango tree nearby. The होउसे itself may then be described as built of bricks with a tiled roofing and green in colour. The former (the mango tree and its branch) stands for the तटस्थलक्षण and the latter for the स्वरूपलक्षण.
It should be noted that the तटस्थलक्षण has nothing to do with the object described though it certainly helps in locating or recognizing it.

Svāhā
(‘that by which gods are invited’)
------------------------------------------
Svāhā or Svāhādevī is the शक्ति (power, consort) of अग्नि (fire-god). She is one of the daughters of दक्ष-प्रजापति. अग्नि gets from her the power to digest the offerings made into him in sacrifices and then carry them to the various deities for whom it is meant. That is why all such offerings should be made with the utterance of the मन्त्र ‘svāhā’.

svara
(‘that which makes sound’)
------------------------------------------
This word has several meanings. In Sanskrit grammar, it represents the thirteen vowels.
In Vedic chanting it stands for the three notes—udātta, अनुदात्त and स्वरित. (See ANUDĀTTA for details.)
In मुसिच्, it denotes the seven basic notes like ṣadja, ऋषभ and so on.

Svargārohaṇaparva
------------------------------------------
This is the last book of the great epic Mahābhārata.
See MAHĀBHĀRATA.

svadharma
(‘one’s own duty’)
------------------------------------------
This is a word that has been specially used in the Bhagavadgītā (2.31, 33; 3.35; 18.47).
It is generally interpreted as sva-वर्ण-आश्रम-धर्म, duties that accrue to one as a result of his belonging to a particular वर्ण (caste) and आश्रम (station in life). अर्जुन was क्षत्त्रिय and a गृहस्थ or a householder. It was his स्वधर्म or ordained duty to fight the evil forces and defend the good.
Of course it should be noted that स्वधर्म must first be धर्म! Otherwise, a thief may declare that stealing is his स्वधर्म!

Svastisūkta
(‘hymn of auspiciousness’)
------------------------------------------
The five mantras of the Ṛgveda (5.51.11-15) together are known as the Svastisūkta since each verse begins with the word ‘svasti’ (= auspiciousness).
It is generally chanted at the time of consecrating the image of विष्णु by tying a strip of cloth (sanctified by this hymn) to its hand.
The deities who are praised and whose blessings are solicited here are: The अश्विन्स्; अदिति (the मोथेर् of gods); पूषन्; हेअवेन् and Earth; वायु (god of wind); सोम; बृहस्पति (teacher of gods); Ādityas; विश्वेदेवस्; अग्नि (fire-god); ऋभुस् (a class of gods who were originally human beings); रुद्र; Mitrā-वरुण; and इन्द्र.
The three verses (13 to 15) are repeated to cure the sacrificer if he becomes ill.
The last मन्त्र (the 15th) can be repeated to overcome the obstacles and dangers while on tour.

svayamācāryas
(‘self-appointed teachers’)
------------------------------------------
Ramānuja (A.

-1137) did not appoint any single person as the next pontiff to succeed him. Instead, he selected 74 pious householder disciples and gave them the power to spread the philosophy of Viśiṣṭādvaita and the religion of श्रीवैष्णविस्म्. These 74 came to be known as ‘svayamācāryas’. They were not only great scholars but also great devotees committed to the श्रीवैष्णविस्म् sect.
They could grant पञ्चसṁस्कारस् (See PAÑCASAṀSKĀRAS.) and mantropadeśa (giving the famous mantras like the अष्टाक्षरी) to disciples.
They were also expected to expound the scriptures according to Rāmānuja’s philosophy.

svāyambhuvaliṅga
(‘self-manifested लिङ्ग [of शिव]’)
------------------------------------------
Śivaliṅgas—emblems of god Śiva—are of several types. According to one classification, by the Suprabhedāgama (paṭala 33), three types of liṅgas are uttamottama or the very best. They are दिव्य (divine, worshipped by gods like ब्रह्मा and विष्णु), pūrva (extremely ancient) and svāyambhuva (self manifested).
Svāyambhuvaliṅgas are not carved or made by human beings or sages or demons, but have manifested by themselves.
See also LIṄGA.

svarūpaśakti
------------------------------------------
This is one of the three śaktis or powers of Śrī कृष्ण who is ब्रह्मन् Himself.
See ACINTYABHEDĀBHEDA SCHOOL.

svādhyāya
(‘repeated study’)
------------------------------------------
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.9,11) stresses the importance of स्वाध्याय very much.
Svādhyāya is the repeated study and understanding of one’s own branch of the Veda. Since a student of Vedic knowledge is expected to teach it to others and thus keep up the continuity of that tradition, a thorough study of the same is greatly stressed.
The subjects of study may include other branches of learning also such as the वेदाङ्गस्, itihāsas and पुराणस्.
Sometimes the word is interpreted as जप (repetition) of God’s name or any मन्त्र (sacred formula).

svarita
(‘falling’)
------------------------------------------
See ANUDĀTTA for details.

Svadhā
------------------------------------------
Svadhā or Svadhādevī was one of the daughters of Dakṣaprajāpati and had been married to the seven पितृस् or manes viz., Agniṣvāttas, Barhiṣadas, Somapās, यम, Anala, सोम, and अर्यमन्. The ड़ोओद् that is offered to them in śrāddhas should be accompanied by the मन्त्र ‘svadhā’. Then only they can get the same.
Obviously this is a symbolical concept. When the मन्त्र ‘svadhā’ is uttered while offering the piṇḍas (rice-balls), it will induce the necessary power into them so as to be received by the पितृस् (the souls of the dead ancestors).

Svayamprabhā
(‘[one who] is self-shining’)
------------------------------------------
Svayamprabhā was the daughter of the sage Śāṇḍilya—hence known as Śāṇḍili also—and was a friend of Hemā, an apsaras (celestial nymph). They lived in a beautiful cave created by मय, a divine architect. When Hemā left for हेअवेन् स्वयम्प्रभा was taking care of the cave.
While searching for सीता, हनुमान् and other monkeys entered this cave and were entertained by her.
Once गरुड offended her and lost his wings by her curse. Later he apologised and got them back.

svapna
(‘dreams’)
------------------------------------------
See AVASTHĀTRAYA and DREAMS.

Svapneśvara
------------------------------------------
The Śāṇḍilya Bhaktisūtras—also known as the Śāṇḍilya-śata-sūtrīyam—has two well-known commentaries: the Bhāṣya of स्वप्नेश्वर and the Bhakticandrikā of Nārāyaṇatīrtha.
Svapneśvara must have existed sometime during the period 14th to the 17th century A. D., much nearer to the 14th.
He belonged to Gauḍadeśa or Bengal. He was the son of Jaleśvara and grandson of Viśārada. Jaleśvara was the commander-in-chief of the king of Bengal.
Nothing more is known about him except that he wrote two more treatises—the Nyāyatattvanikaṣa and the Vedāntatattvanikaṣa. Unfortunately neither work is available now.
His commentary on शाण्डिल्य’s Bhakti-sūtras is simple, natural and direct.

Svāmi-Nārāyaṇa
(A.

-1830)
------------------------------------------
Svāmi-Nārāyana, the founder of the Svāmi-नारायणी sect of reformed वैष्णविस्म्, was born in A.

as the second son of Hariprasād Pāṇḍe and Bālādevī in Chapaiyā (near अयोध्या in Uttar Pradesh). He was named Ghana-śyāma.
Being educated by his ड़थेर्, he showed a remarkable mastery over the Hindu scriptures even at the tender age of six. When he was nine years, both the parents passed away leaving him to the care of his elder brother Rāmapratāpa and aunt Suvāsinī.
At the age of eleven he renounced his hearth and home and started roaming about like a mendicant monk. In his sojourn through Nepal he came across Gopālayogi, a highly evolved spiritual सोउल्, who trained him in the योग techniques of पतञ्जलि’s aṣṭāṅgayoga. The गुरु gave him the new name नीलकण्ठ-ब्रह्मचारिन्.
After visiting Bengal and Orissa he then travelled towards the south of the Indian peninsula right up to कन्याकुमारी. Returning from there, he proceeded towards Maharashtra and then to Gujarat. He finally landed at the village Loj, ending his long spiritual journey.
Very soon he was adopted as a disciple by Svāmi रामानन्द, a well-known Vaiṣṇava saint of the times, and became his favourite. Actually the Svāmi had known through his yogic powers not only about the arrival of this disciple but also about his intrinsic greatness.
On an auspicious day रामानन्द gave नीलकण्ठ the vows of भागवत religion (of devotion to Śrī कृष्ण) and also of सṁन्यास. नीलकण्ठ now became Svāmi Sahajānanda with an additional name ‘Nārāyaṇamuni’.
Gradually, the name Svāminārāyaṇa became more common and well-known.
Svāmi रामानन्द took great care of Svāminārāyaṇa and groomed him to become the next head of the group or sect he had built up, known as the Satsaṅga. The actual abbotship was transferred to him during the last part of the year A.

.
Svāminārāyaṇa initiated many revolutionary steps to purify the Satsaṅga from inside and spread the भागवत religion extensively, especially in Gujarat. His personal magnetism and divine powers brought to him lakhs of devotees and disciples, who remained loyal to him throughout their life.
He reformed the lives of many people including the members of a notorious criminal gang known as Khatris.
His disciples were divided into two categories, the satsaṅgis and the साधुस्. Householders and other who were not साधुस् or मोन्क्स्, belonged to the first category. The साधुस् or the monastic members belonged to the second category.
He prescribed pañcaśīlas or five rules of conduct for both the groups. The first group was expected to abstain from stealing, अदुल्तेर्य्, eating flesh, drinking and eating the ड़ोओद् offered by persons belonging to castes lower than one’s own. As for the second group comprising मोन्क्स् the following rules were prescribed: give up worldly desires and greed; not catering to the tastes of the tongue or the quality of ड़ोओद्; renounce egoism and delusion.
This was further buttressed by many more stringent rules. Transgressors were dealt with very severely.
Svāminārāyaṇa established six Vaiṣṇava temples in six places as follows:
Naranārāyaṇa temples in Ahmedabad and Bhuj; Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa temple at Vaḍatāla; Madanmohan temple at Dhūlera; Rādhāramaṇa temple at Jūnā-gaḍh and Gopīnātha temple at Gaḍhaḍā.
The image in the last one resembles him and his spirit had been infused into it.
The philosophy of Svāminārāyaṇa can be briefly stated as follows:
The highest Truth or God is Akṣaradhāma (the Indestructible Abode) or चैतन्य or ब्रह्मन् or पुरुषोत्तम. He is the creator, sustainer and destroyer of the universe. He incarnates himself as राम, कृष्ण and other gods.
The जीव or the individual सोउल् is different from God and is subjected to the law of कर्म. The jīvas are infinite in number.
Māyā is the power of God comprising the three guṇas (sattva, रजस् and तमस्) with which He creates the world. It is the same māyā that binds the जीव to the body and the world.
God can be realised by भक्ति or devotion and nāmajapa or repetition of the divine name. In fact the word ‘Svāmi-नारायण’ is itself the sacred मन्त्र, divine name, that has to be used for repetition.
In मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्, the जीव gets a divine, eternal body and lives in the divine abode, serving God.
Svāminārāyaṇa practically accepts the philosophy of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) in his teachings.
His वैष्णविस्म् accords an important place to all the five gods of traditional हिन्दुइस्म्, viz., विष्णु, शिव, देवी, गणपति and सूर्य.
He has left two works for the posterity: the Śikṣāpatrī (in 212 ślokas) and the Vacanāmṛtam. The former is his own work whereas the latter is a compilation of his teachings by his disciples.
The first ten ślokas of the Śikṣāpatrī give a general introduction. The next part comprising the ślokas 11 to 122 describe the sāmānyadharmas, duties common to all persons. The last part (123 to 212) deals with the viśeṣadharmas, duties and responsibilities assigned to various groups of people like the householders, religious teachers, kings, married women as also widows, and मोन्क्स्. Some of the revolutionary steps taken by Svāminārāyaṇa included building of a large number of small temples especially in villages, allowing women also to worship in those temples, giving सṁन्यास or monastic vows and robes to deserving women, appointing ācāryas or pious householder-teachers to guide the householder devotees and so on.
Over the years, the Svāminārāyaṇa sect has grown into a mighty organisation with several branch centres in India and abroad. These centres are undertaking many public service activities including the running of educational institutions and hospitals as also rural welfare schemes.

Svarodayavijñāna
(‘science of prediction depending on the breather’s health’)
------------------------------------------
The air we breathe in, the प्राण (vital air or energy) in the body, and the मिन्द् are interconnected. Hence by controlling the act of breathing which is technically called स्वर, it is possible to control health, achieve longevity and predict certain things.
Normally, breathing takes place through one nostril at a time and it changes over to the other after an hour. When it is in the left, it is connected with the iḍā-nāḍī and when in the right, with the पिङ्गला-nāḍi. When it is flowing smoothly through both, it is connected with the सुषुम्ना-nāḍi.
This science teaches the methods of changing the स्वर (or respiration) from one to the other.
Perfection in this science can endow the person with several supernatural powers.

Svarṇagaurīvrata
------------------------------------------
The स्वर्णगौरीव्रत is observed on the Bhādrapada śukla tṛtīyā day. It is mostly confined to the women of the Karnataka region. It is believed that गौरी or पार्वती comes to her parent’s होउसे on this day and that गणेश comes there the next day to escort her back!
Gaurī is worshipped in a clay image or a कलश installed in a मण्डप (a small pavilion). The married women who observe it, fast for the day and offer worship with 16 उपचारस्. They pray for health, sons, wealth and longevity of their husbands. At the end they have to do उद्यापन by donating 16 baskets each filled with sixteen edibles and covered with a cloth, to ब्राह्मण ladies and their husbands.

svayaṁvara
(‘choosing the husband [by a girl] by her own choice’)
------------------------------------------
In the olden days, if a girl who had attained puberty was not married off to a suitable young man by her ड़थेर् or guardian, she would wait for three years and then choose her husband herself. This was a well-known variety of स्वयṁवर common to all castes. सावित्री choosing सत्यवान् is quoted as an example for this kind.
But the svayaṁvaras described in the two great epics are often more elaborate and spectacular affairs. They were confined to the royal families only. In some cases, the svayaṁvaras did not depend upon the will of the bride at all, but upon some heroic deed set by her ड़थेर्, as in the case of सीता and द्रौपदी.
The svayaṁvaras of दमयन्ती and Indumati may also be quoted as examples.
The writers of धर्मशास्त्रस् include this under the category of गान्धर्व विवाह.

svastika
------------------------------------------
The स्वस्तिक is a symbol of auspiciousness (svasti = auspiciousness). It has been used as a symbol of the sun or of विष्णु or even of गणेश. It also represents the world-wheel, the eternally changing world, round a fixed, unchanging centre or God.
Svastika marks depicted on doors or walls of building or on animals, are believed to protect them from the wrath of evil spirits or furies of nature.
